item.title: node_e2e: Cleanup configuration and rename jenkins/ directory

detail.title: node_e2e: Cleanup configuration and rename jenkins/ directory
detail.body:
/kind cleanup
/sig node
/area test
/priority important-longterm
/assign

Currently, node_e2e configuration exists in the `jenkins/` directory underneath node_e2e. This directory is a hangover from the time before Kubernetes migrated to Prow. This directory is regularly a point of contention when adding new features to tests, and causes confusion to people trying to make changes to them.

We should remove the unused portions of this directory and rename it to something more useful (`e2e_node/configuration`?) to simplify future changes while maintaining the current developer workflow.

This is going to involve coordinating a couple of things between k/k and k/test-infra to ensure that we do not cause a break in tests during the migration process and to not break running tests against older release branches.

My naive suggestion for handling this would be:

- [ ] Remove unused code from jenkins/
- [ ] Create a copy of the jenkins/ directory with the new name
- [ ] Update test-infra to reference the new paths, duplicating configurations where necessary to preserve jobs for older branches
- [ ] Remove the jenkins/ directory

(@spiffxp / @dims might have better suggestions for how to handle this?)

item.title: Crash in TestGetContainerOOMScoreAdjust

detail.title: Crash in TestGetContainerOOMScoreAdjust
detail.body:
### Which jobs are failing?

pkg/kubelet/qos

### Which tests are failing?

`TestGetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` in `pkg/kubelet/qos`
I transformed that testcase into a fuzz driver and tested it with [[go-fuzz](https://github.com/dvyukov/go-fuzz)](https://github.com/dvyukov/go-fuzz)
It crash with "integer divide by zero" when some argument related data are fuzzed.

### Since when has it been failing?

Always

### Testgrid link

_No response_

### Reason for failure (if possible)

_No response_

### Anything else we need to know?

Simplified PoC code is here:

```go
	test := oomTest{
		pod:             &cpuLimit,
		memoryCapacity:  0,
		lowOOMScoreAdj:  999,
		highOOMScoreAdj: 999,
	}
	GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust(test.pod, &test.pod.Spec.Containers[0], test.memoryCapacity)
```

and it crashed as:

```
panic: runtime error: integer divide by zero [recovered]
	panic: runtime error: integer divide by zero

goroutine 19 [running]:
testing.tRunner.func1.2({0xaf6ea0, 0x11714b0})
	/home/gogen/.local/go/src/testing/testing.go:1209 +0x24e
testing.tRunner.func1()
	/home/gogen/.local/go/src/testing/testing.go:1212 +0x218
panic({0xaf6ea0, 0x11714b0})
	/home/gogen/.local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:1038 +0x215
k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/qos.GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust(0x1179620, 0x11856e0, 0x0)
	/home/gogen/workspace/gowork/src/topproj/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/qos/policy.go:63 +0x2d5
k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/qos.FuzzTestGetContainerOOMScoreAdjust({0xc000230400, 0x0, 0x200})
	/home/gogen/workspace/gowork/src/topproj/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/qos/policy_test.go_TestGetContainerOOMScoreAdjust_test.go:79 +0x2b5
```

### 

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig

It's better to handle the exception case instead of panic

detail.title: Probe tests are flaking often on some jobs
detail.body:
### Which jobs are failing?

It is a follow up from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115856#issuecomment-1447807752

Looks like liveness probes are failing with different symptoms. Looks like the failures are happening for  different probe types.

### Which tests are failing?

https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?test=liveness 

Preliminary analysis indicates it may be a Windows issue:

/sig windows
/sig node

### Since when has it been failing?

Don't know.

### Testgrid link

_No response_

### Reason for failure (if possible)

One test failure from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115856#issuecomment-1447807752. Seems like probes worked OK and reported failure. But kubelet didn't react on this failure and haven't restarted the Container at all.

There are other cases when for some reason kubelet keeps restarting container, even before any probes were started. Perhaps some issue with agnhost.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig windows
/sig node

item.title: Enhance pod lifecycle transitions testing and documentation

detail.title: Enhance pod lifecycle transitions testing and documentation
detail.body:
The proposal is to create a collection of tests with the cross linked documentation pages that would demonstrate all interesting behaviors of Pod lifecycle events.

Ideally, docs pages must be at least partially auto-generated off the tests. And tests be cross linked back to the documentation pages.

More details:

- As part of sidecar container KEP we introduced a handy test framework that allows to define the Pod spec and test the sequence of callbacks executed in it: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e_node/container_lifecycle_test.go#L155-L164 Today many tests are in a single file, they can be split apart into separate files under subfolder
- We also have an overview diagram that can be used to identify scenarios: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1e-qJWe6He2qjt0PFiZtocqP8VbkrwKAI9B4X72L0bGk/edit?resourcekey=0-N77W7Q5UHuN5dFtekjmAIA#slide=id.g209315a2632_0_0 The diagram can be an entry-point in the k8s docs to the repository of those behaviors.

/sig node
/kind cleanup
/area test
/priority backlog

detail.title: Clean up features for SIG Node e2e tests
detail.body:
We use features to indicate the environment that is "not standard" for e2e tests - i.e. requires extra configuration beyond feature gates.

This is uber issue to review sig-node features and clean them up:

1. If the Feature is used to indicate just a "category" of tests - remove it
2. If the Feature is used when FeatureGate must be used - replace with the FeatureGate
3. If the Feature truly indicate a special environment, make sure it is well documented and corresponding test lanes are marked appropriately

Once we clear things up we may decide to pass the `Feature` as an argument for the test lane (similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/35531 idea) and have more automated validation that the test requiring the Feature are only run in the test lane implementing this special environment

/sig node
/area test
/kind cleanup
/priority important-longterm
/cc @mariafromano-25  @esotsal

detail.title: [Flaking test] [InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Pod Resize deferred tests are flaking
detail.body:
https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?test=pod-resize-retry-deferred

Looks like they've been flaking for a while. I think its most likely an issue with the way the test is written than an issue with the feature.

comments.body:
/sig node

/help
if anyone wants to take a stab at root-causing before I get to it

@natasha41575: 
	This request has been marked as needing help from a contributor.

### Guidelines

>

>


Instructions for interacting with me using PR comments are available [here](https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/pull-requests.md).  If you have questions or suggestions related to my behavior, please file an issue against the [kubernetes-sigs/prow](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prow/issues/new?title=Prow%20issue:) repository.
</details>

I can help investigate this! 

Looking at the test code in `test/e2e/node/pod_resize.go`, I've identified some potential timing issues:

## Observations:

1. **The `waitForPodDeferred()` function** (line 1276-1280) uses `f.Timeouts.PodStart` as the timeout, which may not be appropriate for deferred resize scenarios where resource allocation can take longer.

2. **Race condition between resource calculation and resize**: In all three deferred tests, there's a sequence like:
   - Calculate available node resources
   - Create/patch multiple pods
   - Wait for deferred status
   
   Between steps, other pods or system processes might consume resources, causing the expected "deferred" state to be different than anticipated.

3. **Test 1 potential issue** (line 691-817): The test calculates `nodeAvailableMilliCPU2` but then creates pod3 which might affect the actual available resources before the resize patch is applied.

## Suggested Fixes:

1. **Add retry logic with backoff** instead of a single wait
2. **Use a more appropriate timeout** - maybe `f.Timeouts.PodStartSlow` or a custom timeout for resize operations
3. **Add resource availability checks** right before the resize patch to ensure the test assumptions still hold
4. **Add logging** of actual vs expected resource values when the test fails

Would you like me to prepare a PR with these fixes? I can start with adding better logging and adjusting the timeout values.

/assign @oyiz-michael

I have some questions, maybe you can elaborate more on your observations

> The waitForPodDeferred() function (line 1276-1280) uses f.Timeouts.PodStart as the timeout, which may not be appropriate for deferred resize scenarios where resource allocation can take longer.

Why wouldn't PodStart be appropriate as a timeout? The allocation manager shouldn't take that long to run and decide whether to allocate or defer the resize. If it is actually taking longer than pod starting, we should try to find out why.

> Between steps, other pods or system processes might consume resources, causing the expected "deferred" state to be different than anticipated.

Deferred state is calculated based on the sum of other pod requests. Unless other pods are being created, deleted, or resized unexpectedly, I don't think it should change the deferred result. I think of the observations you listed, this one might be a feasible culprit. Have you found logs showing that other create/delete/resize operations are happening at the same time? 

> The test calculates nodeAvailableMilliCPU2 but then creates pod3 which might affect the actual available resources before the resize patch is applied.

I don't really understand this one. pod3's resources are calculated based off of `nodeAvailableMilliCPU2`, so `nodeAvailableMilliCPU2` necessarily needs to be calculated before creating pod3. Have you looked at the logs or anything to see if the resized calculation is wrong, and if so why does it only happen sometimes? 

I think we need a better understanding of what could be causing the issue before we start writing a PR. More logging is fine if you have looked at the logs and found a specific gap that prevents us from root causing the issue.

/triage accepted
/priority important-soon
cc @esotsal
also ccing @hshiina. No pressure  at all,  but if you are interested, you have helped a lot with deflaking some other tests so your input might be helpful here too :)

I took a look again and the aggregated error dashboard and I changed my mind about the priority. These tests are really long and complicated, and they are actually not flaking that much relative to all they are doing so I don't think it needs to necessarily be fixed before GA. It would still be good to deflake though if we can.

/remove-priority important-soon

item.title: Make sig-node CI test coverage adhere to defined guidance

detail.title: Make sig-node CI test coverage adhere to defined guidance
detail.body:
A couple of years ago, we started a project to define guidance for sig node tests. This is written here: https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/3665d0cddb9b83302ab3463b599156ae79a16ef8/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/README.md

However, it doesn't appear that [our testgrid](https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node) adheres to this guidance.

This is an umbrella issue for all that needs to be done to make it so. We need to:

- [ ] Understand if new testing guidance (like [this email](https://groups.google.com/a/kubernetes.io/g/dev/c/wyyXD1aKUKE/m/libCYUzDBAAJ?utm_medium=email&utm_source=footer)) changes any of our past plans
- [ ] Audit the existing test job names, ensuring they follow [the naming convention](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/3665d0cddb9b83302ab3463b599156ae79a16ef8/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/README.md#naming-convention).
- [ ] Audit the existing test lanes, ensuring they follow the naming conventions and contain the test jobs they are supposed to per the [test tab guidance](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/3665d0cddb9b83302ab3463b599156ae79a16ef8/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/README.md#1-sig-node-default-ie-rename-sig-node-release-blocking).
- [ ] For any lanes / jobs that are not specified in the guidance doc, take a decision on whether the job / lane is useful and whether any changes are needed. Update the doc accordingly.
- [ ] There is some obsolete guidance in the doc (i.e. cgroupsv1), we should update the tests and docs accordingly.

state.title: Make sig-node CI test coverage adhere to defined guidance
state.description:
A couple of years ago, we started a project to define guidance for sig node tests. This is written here: https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/3665d0cddb9b83302ab3463b599156ae79a16ef8/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/README.md

However, it doesn't appear that [our testgrid](https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node) adheres to this guidance.

This is an umbrella issue for all that needs to be done to make it so. We need to:

- [ ] Understand if new testing guidance (like [this email](https://groups.google.com/a/kubernetes.io/g/dev/c/wyyXD1aKUKE/m/libCYUzDBAAJ?utm_medium=email&utm_source=footer)) changes any of our past plans
- [ ] Audit the existing test job names, ensuring they follow [the naming convention](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/3665d0cddb9b83302ab3463b599156ae79a16ef8/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/README.md#naming-convention).
- [ ] Audit the existing test lanes, ensuring they follow the naming conventions and contain the test jobs they are supposed to per the [test tab guidance](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/3665d0cddb9b83302ab3463b599156ae79a16ef8/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/README.md#1-sig-node-default-ie-rename-sig-node-release-blocking).
- [ ] For any lanes / jobs that are not specified in the guidance doc, take a decision on whether the job / lane is useful and whether any changes are needed. Update the doc accordingly.
- [ ] There is some obsolete guidance in the doc (i.e. cgroupsv1), we should update the tests and docs accordingly.

I noticed that the **README** already defines a naming convention similar to a manual templating system (e.g., `(pull|ci)-{$cri}-{$cgroup}-{$os}-{$test-type}-release-{$release-branch}`).
I’d like to explore converting this into actual **Go templating** using the existing `config/jobs/templates/ `mechanism in `test-infra`, so that SIG Node job definitions are generated automatically from structured data rather than manually repeated YAMLs.
This would keep consistency with the documented pattern, reduce duplication, and make updates (like adding new release branches or OS combinations) trivial.

- Only 7 of those 34 are attributed to the `with swap stress LimitedSwap should be able to use more than the node memory capacity` row. The other ~27 are job-level failures (`kubetest2.Test` / `.Overall` = `exit status 255`) with no test row marked failed at all.

**Why the job-level failures don't show up as test failures**

In those runs the same test is in progress when the kubelet on the Ubuntu node dies mid-test. The build log shows the swap stress pod ramping up, then the kubelet health check flipping to `EOF` and then `connection refused`, and the run never produces junit output:

```
STEP: swap usage found: 115757056 bytes @ 09/14/26 07:00:41.539
I0914 07:00:48.925685 helper.go:242] Health check on "http://127.0.0.1:10248/healthz" failed, error=Head "http://127.0.0.1:10248/healthz": EOF
I0914 07:00:50.254286 helper.go:242] Health check on "http://127.0.0.1:10248/healthz" failed, error=Head "http://127.0.0.1:10248/healthz": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:10248: connect: connection refused
...
E0914 07:48:44.634862 ssh.go:148] failed to run SSH command: out: ls: cannot access '/tmp/node-e2e-20260914T062612/results/junit*': No such file or directory
F0914 07:49:17.293976 node.go:498] failed to run ginkgo tester: exit status 2
```

Because there is no junit, TestGrid has nothing to attribute the failure to, so these runs only count against the `.Overall` row. This is the same signature as the original report here (`expected kubelet to be in healthy state` in AfterEach), just one step further: the node is unreachable for the rest of the run instead of recovering.

Example runs with this pattern (all Ubuntu image `ubuntu-gke-2404-1-34-amd64-v20260912`):

- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-swap-conformance-ubuntu-serial/2099382137948999680
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-swap-conformance-ubuntu-serial/2099019746828619776
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-swap-conformance-ubuntu-serial/2098777900630151168
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-swap-conformance-ubuntu-serial/2098354394083889152

For comparison, `ci-node-crio-swap-serial` (CRI-O, same `[Feature:NodeSwap]` focus) is 10/10 green over the same window, so this looks specific to the containerd/Ubuntu configuration or the Ubuntu image rather than the swap test logic itself.

Given the ~38% failure rate this is closer to a failing job than a flake. Should we bump priority, or consider skipping the stress test on this job until the node crash is understood?

/cc @iholder101 @isumitsolanki
@isumitsolanki are you still working on this? It has been quiet for 74 days. If not, please `/unassign` so someone else can pick it up. No worries either way.

/triage accepted

/assign @pravk03
The failure is not arm specific. This is also failing on x86 - https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-containerd-node-e2e-serial-ec2

I haven't looked into the exact topology of the machine where the test failed, but the problem seems to be that currently we hardcode the exact CPU IDs we expect the Kubelet to assign.

Instead of checking for specific CPU ID's in e2e tests which may be brittle with different architectures, we could verify the CPU counts and verify that the assigned CPUs do not overlap. We can test the exact allocation logic and specific CPU IDs in unit tests, where the hardware topology is fully controlled ?

  gomega.Eventually(ctx, func(g gomega.Gomega) {

I dug into one specific failure to figure out whether this is a flaky timeout or something real, and it's real — here's the root cause.

I traced build [`2099502935326068736`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-containerd/2099502935326068736) (COS run, Sep 14 2026), where `RestartAllContainersWithKubeletRestarts` / "during startup" failed with `[FAILED] Timed out after 180.001s ... not all containers are running`.

**Timeline (from `containerd.log` / `kubelet.log` on the COS node):**

- `15:58:47.807` — test triggers `STEP: restarting kubelet`
- `15:58:47.907` — old kubelet process shuts down
- `15:58:48.037` — new kubelet process comes up
- `15:58:49.064` — new kubelet receives the pod fresh from the API server and treats it as "synced for the first time"
- `15:58:49.065` — new kubelet decides `"Pod is terminal"` → `"Pod directory completed naturally and should now terminate"`
- `15:58:49.065 – 15:58:50.172` — pod gets torn down in two passes: containers destroyed and volumes unmounted, then a housekeeping pass finds the pod "orphaned," destroys the last sandbox container, removes the cgroups, and broadcasts `"Pod removed"` at `15:58:50.171611`
- `16:01:52.986` — test finally times out waiting for "all containers running" — which was never going to happen, since the pod itself was already deleted just over 3 minutes earlier

**Root cause:**

Right before the kubelet restart, every container in the pod had a status like:
lastState.terminated{exitCode: 137, reason: "RestartingAllContainers", message: "The container is removed because RestartAllContainers in place"}


That's the feature's own signal for "this container isn't done — it's paused mid-coordinated-restart, please recreate it." The old kubelet process understood that and was actively recreating containers (it had already recreated `init` right before it got killed).

The new kubelet process doesn't. When it rebuilds pod state from scratch after restarting, it sees a pod whose containers all exited and applies its normal completion logic — it concludes the pod's work is done and deletes it, instead of resuming the restart.

So this isn't a slow-recovery issue, and no timeout value fixes it — the pod is gone well before the 180s wait even starts. The gap is specifically in how `RestartAllContainersOnContainerExits`/`ContainerRestartRules` state survives a kubelet process restart; the "mid-restart, don't clean me up" intent doesn't seem to be checkpointed or restored when the pod worker rebuilds state fresh.

This likely explains the flakiness too — it would only reproduce when the kubelet restart lands in the narrow window where containers are marked "paused for restart" but not yet recreated. I've only deep-traced this one instance so far; haven't yet confirmed the other historical failures show the identical teardown pattern, but the failure signature (timeout at the exact 180s boundary) is consistent with it.

I'll pick this up and look into a fix for the pod-worker's restart-recovery path.

  - Pod object-count and compute quotas: requests/limits cpu & memory, requests.hugepages-*, the Constraints "must specify requests" denial, and delete-driven replenishment (a create is allowed after one pod is deleted).
  - Terminated-pod exclusion: create a pod then set its phase to Succeeded. Check requests.cpu drops to 0 while a count/pods quota stays at 1.
  - Scopes + scope selectors: Terminating/NotTerminating, BestEffort/NotBestEffort, PriorityClass, CrossNamespacePodAffinity.
  - Admission edge cases: dry-run not charged, multiple quotas (most-restrictive wins), limitedResources for a resource the existing test doesn't cover.
  - ResourceQuota object lifecycle: status subresource, Spec.Hard updates, deletecollection.

I believe `ResourceQuota` also caps object counts (count/secrets, count/configmaps, replicationcontrollers/replicasets, custom resources) and storage (PVC requests.storage, per storageclass limits). Should those be tested too?

For the migration of E2E tests if needed, I'm thinking of doing that in a second PR, after adding the new integration tests. Any objections?

item.title: [SIG NODE Discussion] Metrics and dashboards for monitoring SIG-Node CI test failures and bug triage health

detail.title: [SIG NODE Discussion] Metrics and dashboards for monitoring SIG-Node CI test failures and bug triage health
detail.body:
### Context
In the recent SIG-Node CI subgroup meetings (6/10/2026), we discussed the need to better track our CI stability and test degradation over time. 

Currently, we are manually tracking the status of our Testgrid dashboards in a [Spreadsheet Tracker](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1IwONkeXSc2SG_EQMYGRSkfiSWNk8yWLpVhPm-LOTbGM) before every meeting. We document the current status (Passing/Flaky/Failing) of the jobs and link them to tracking GitHub issues, but doing this manually makes it hard to see historic data and trends.

### Goals
We would like to gather community input on what metrics, tooling, and dashboards we should use to automate this monitoring. For starters, we can try to answer questions like:
* How long has a specific test or job been failing?
* Is a recurring failure caused by the same error or a new regression?
* How long do SIG-Node CI bugs remain open?
* How many `important-soon` bugs do we currently have, and what is their average resolution time?
Please recommend any more you think of, open to all suggestions!!

### Existing Efforts & Ideas
* We dug up an [existing dashboard started by dims](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-metrics/failures-latest.html?include=node&sort=days&asc=0), but we need to determine how persistent this data is, how it's generated, and how we can best utilize or adapt it.
* Could we leverage existing Kubernetes `test-infra` tooling (like BigQuery metrics/[Kettle](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/kettle/README.md), `k8s-triage` in the [aggregated failures dashboard](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?sig=node)) to automate the data we currently put in our manual spreadsheet?

### Call to Action
We are opening this issue to invite ideas from the CI/CD community. 
1. What metrics do you think are most important for us to track?
2. Are there existing dashboards or tools in the Kubernetes ecosystem we should be leveraging?
3. Any volunteers interested in helping build out or maintain this reporting?

Please drop your thoughts and suggestions below!

/sig node
cc: @SergeyKanzhelev

comments.body:
/sig node
/sig testing
/triage accepted
/priority backlog
/kind feature
/area test

From today's CI meeting: 
- option 1: look into the source code of Dim's dashboard and make some edits to fit our triage process.
    --> consider: much longer investment in time and effort but could be longer standing solution for the group
- option 2: add the flaky label in test code if we see it fail for over xx amount of days. 
    --> consider: clearly outline how long until we add the label and how long it will take to fix.  
    --> [k8s flaky definition](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/10c089c55c543e702ba7eff26b1e038650fd5da2/contributors/devel/sig-testing/e2e-tests.md?plain=1#L554)

Any thoughts?

I was thinking about it. I have a feeling that splitting the dashboard into reasons will become a never-ending chase of additional dimensions. Keeping it green sounds like a better idea. So I think it is the good idea to start being more aggressive in applying the `[Flaky]` label to tests.

So the goal is to keep all the jobs green. And separately - track ownership and "time to fix" for all flakes. Maybe even cross link all `Flaky` labels with the tracking issues.

This separation will put the right ownership - CI group ownership of keeping test lanes green and finding owners for test failures. And specific components owners responsible for individual tests.

We can extend this model to test definitions by moving continuously failing tests to "Flaky" tab with associated tracking bug and an owner.

Some policy around not moving release blocking tests to Flaky or moving to Flaky and treat fixes as release blocking issues would be needed as well. Not that important for features that are not GA or not yet treated as release blocking.

Quick rundown of what that helper does: it polls every 1s for up to 5s waiting for kubelet to write an ImagePulledRecord at /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled/sha256-<hash>, then moves it aside so a later step can check kubelet's behavior when the record's missing. If nothing shows up in 5s, it just fails.

#138527 got closed by 
#138642, but looking at that PR, it only added debug logging to this wait loop - didn't touch the 5s timeout or actually figure out why the record's sometimes missing. So this was never really fixed, just made easier to see happening.

#138642 caught this in a recent run (2026-07-25, ~12:40 UTC) that wasn't visible back when 
#138527 was filed:

  .../pulled/sha256-fbeb66043fabeed6f125049e44aef32e0b8f9e657a240b5a2091b292bab530f2:
    {"kind":"ImagePulledRecord", ..., "lastUpdatedTime":"2026-07-25T14:26:20Z", ...}
]

Would be good to get sig-node's take on whether that's expected - if so, the fix is probably on the test's assumptions, not the timeout.

item.title: No e2e coverage for readiness probes during graceful pod termination

detail.title: No e2e coverage for readiness probes during graceful pod termination
detail.body:
### What happened?

#140881 was a total loss of exec readiness probing during the entire graceful termination window, shipped in v1.35.0 and caught by a user, not by CI. Nothing in the e2e suite asserts anything about probes after a pod's `deletionTimestamp` is set.

`test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go` covers startup, ordering, timeouts, restart counts, and readiness before delete, but every readiness assertion happens while the pod is running normally. `test/e2e/node/pod_termination*.go` and the graceful-shutdown tests cover termination but assert on lifecycle, not readiness. So the probe path and the termination path are each well covered and the intersection is not covered at all.

The unit regression test added in #140882 (`TestProbeWorkersSurviveSyncContextCancellation`) pins the specific context plumbing, but it fakes the pod worker's cancellation. It would not catch a different regression that breaks probing during termination somewhere else in the stack, e.g. in `pod_workers.go` or in the CRI call path.

Filed as a follow-up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140882#discussion_r3659065740, per @SergeyKanzhelev's request to keep the e2e work out of the backport-able patch.

### What did you expect to happen?

An e2e test that deletes a pod whose readiness probe starts failing on SIGTERM and asserts the pod's `Ready` condition flips to `False` well before the grace period ends.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

N/A, this is a coverage gap. To confirm it: revert #140882 on master and run `test/e2e/common/node` plus the node e2e probe suites. Everything passes.

### Anything else we need to know?

Sketch of the test, matching the manual repro in #140881:

- busybox container that touches `/tmp/ready`, traps `TERM` with `rm -f /tmp/ready; sleep 300`, then idles.
- exec readiness probe `cat /tmp/ready`, `periodSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 1`.
- `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`.
- Wait for `Ready=True`, delete the pod, then assert `Ready=False` within ~10s, with the pod still in `Terminating`.

Two traps worth writing into the test as comments so the next person does not re-learn them:

1. Assert on the pod's `Ready` condition, not on EndpointSlice membership. The `deletionTimestamp` withdraws the endpoint immediately regardless of readiness, which masks the bug completely.
2. The grace period has to be long enough that the container is still alive when the assertion runs, otherwise the test passes for the wrong reason.

Coverage worth adding beyond the base case, in rough priority order:

1. exec readiness probe during termination (the actual regression).
2. HTTP readiness probe during termination. Not affected by #140881 because the HTTP prober does not take the probe context, but it is the same contract and nothing pins it.
3. Readiness recorded during termination is reflected in the pod status, so a preStop hook that intentionally fails readiness behaves as documented.

Home is probably `test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go`. It should not be a `ConformanceIt` initially, since it asserts kubelet timing behavior rather than an API guarantee, but it is a reasonable promotion candidate later.

Happy to take this one. PR to follow once #140882 merges, so the test lands against the fixed behavior rather than a known-red baseline.

Related: #140881, #140882, #130487

```console

Server Version: v1.35.0
```

</details>

Gap exists on master and all supported branches.

comments.body:
/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm
🤖 please dig into this. look deep into each ci job that failed by pulling down logs and figure out why things are flaky.

## Triage: `ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial` — three unrelated failure modes, not one flake

I pulled logs for **every** failing build in the GCS-retained window (2026‑07‑11 → 07‑29) and classified each by root cause. The "cluster doesn't come up" framing conflates **three independent problems**. The specific build linked in the issue is only the least interesting one.

### Failure-mode breakdown (27 reds inspected in the window)

| Mode | Count | What actually happened | Class |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. t2a VM STOCKOUT** | ~9 | GCE can't allocate the `t2a-standard-2` VM in `us-central1-a`; VM never boots | Infra/capacity |
| **B. 3h suite hang** | ~16 | VM boots, ginkgo launched over SSH, then **node goes silent** — prow hard-kills at the 180m decoration timeout | The real bug |
| **C. Single reboot/static-pod test fail** | ~2 | Suite runs to completion, 1 of ~190 specs fails | Known flake, arch-independent |

### Mode A — the build in the issue is a pure GCE stockout (not k8s)
The linked build [2082290551972958208](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial/2082290551972958208) ran only ~7.5 min and ended with:
```
ERROR: (gcloud.compute.instances.create) ...
code: ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED_WITH_DETAILS
message: A t2a-standard-2 VM instance is currently unavailable in the us-central1-a zone.
         Consider ... us-central1-f, us-central1-b ... (state:STOCKOUT ...)
```
The [job config](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/node-kubelet.yaml) pins `--gcp-zone=us-central1-a` and `t2a-standard-2` (real arm64 hardware, `k8s-infra-prow-build` cluster — **not emulated**). Arm `t2a` capacity in a single zone is thin, so ~1/3 of the reds are just GCE telling us to pick another zone. **Fix:** multi-zone fallback (the error literally names `us-central1-f`/`-b` as having capacity) or a zone rotation in the image-config. This is self-resolving and not a code regression.

### Mode B — the dominant failure: the suite silently hangs until prow kills it at 3h
This is what's actually worth fixing and produced the long streaks (e.g. **07‑15→07‑17: ~14 consecutive reds**; 07‑22: 5 reds). Signature in every Mode‑B build, e.g. [2081745699879260160](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial/2081745699879260160):
```
... ssh ... ./ginkgo -focus="[Serial]" ... e2e_node.test ...      <- suite launched over SSH
{"level":"error","msg":"Process did not finish before 3h0m0s timeout"}   <- prow entrypoint kill
```
Decisive evidence — **artifacts of a hung build vs a healthy one**:
- Hung build artifacts: `build-log.txt`, `junit_runner.xml` (empty), `metadata.json` — **and nothing else**.
- Healthy build ([2082472497290153984](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial/2082472497290153984)): full per‑node tree — `serial-1.log`, `kubelet.log`, `containerd.log`, `*-ginkgo.log`, `junit_ubuntu01.xml`.

So the node boots, ginkgo starts over SSH, and then **no test output ever streams back and no per-node logs are ever collected** — the node/SSH channel wedges mid-run and the runner blocks until the 180m guillotine. Because the kill is external, there is **no junit and no serial console to post-mortem** — that's the core diagnosability gap.

Two config facts that make this worse and are independently fixable:
- **Timeout mismatch:** decoration `timeout: 180m` but kubetest2 is passed `--timeout=4h0m0s` and ginkgo `-timeout=24h`. The inner timeouts can never fire — prow's 180m always wins, guaranteeing a log-less kill instead of a graceful ginkgo timeout that would dump node logs.
- Every Mode‑B log shows early `ssh: connect ... port 22: Connection refused` / `Permission denied (publickey)` during boot (retried OK), consistent with a flaky serial/SSH path on these t2a images rather than a specific test.

**Recommended next step (owner: SIG Node):** align the timeouts so ginkgo self-terminates and uploads node logs *before* the 180m kill (set kubetest2/ginkgo timeout well under 180m), so the next hang produces a `serial-1.log`/`kubelet.log` to root-cause. Right now every hang is an evidence black hole.

### Mode C — a known, arch-independent test flake (not arm-specific)
The 2 builds that ran to completion failed a single spec at `mirror_pod_test.go:930` ([2080897853596635136](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial/2080897853596635136)) or `static_pod_test.go` ([2078655240525058048](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial/2078655240525058048)) — kubelet-restart/mirror-pod timing. **This reproduces on native amd64:** `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-serial` build [2082439532740874240](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-serial/2082439532740874240) failed the *same* `mirror_pod_test.go:930` spec on 07‑29. So this is not an arch/"slow VM" issue — it's the previously-tracked static/mirror-pod flake family (cf. #137737). The amd64 native serial job is otherwise ~all green, which **rules out a code regression** as the cause of the arm64 reds — the arm64-specific pain is Modes A and B (infra), not test code.

### Bottom line
- **Not a single flake, and not a k8s code regression.** No commit-window bisect applies — the amd64 native equivalent is green.
- **~60% of reds = Mode B** (suite hangs → 3h prow kill, no logs). This is the real actionable item and needs the timeout re-alignment above so it becomes diagnosable.
- **~33% = Mode A** (t2a stockout in `us-central1-a`) — fix with multi-zone fallback.
- **~7% = Mode C** — the existing static/mirror-pod test flake, arch-independent.

If someone can land the timeout fix, the next Mode‑B occurrence will actually leave a `kubelet.log`/serial console behind and we can finish the root cause. Happy to open the test-infra PR for the timeout alignment + zone fallback if SIG Node wants it.

item.title: [Failing-test]: investigate host memory used while resolving Ubuntu images for DRA node jobs

detail.title: [Failing-test]: investigate host memory used while resolving Ubuntu images for DRA node jobs
detail.body:
## Current status

The root cause has been confirmed.

`getGCEImage` used:

    gcloud compute images list --format=json --project=<project>

and buffered and unmarshaled the complete project listing.

For `ubuntu-os-gke-cloud`, the real Prow measurement was:

- 12,558 images
- 283 MiB JSON
- runner VmHWM: 1,067 MiB
- lookup: 44.6s

The equivalent COS path returned 234 images / 1.5 MiB and the runner peaked at 43 MiB.

kubernetes/kubernetes#141590 added a gcloud-side family filter before the output reaches `exec.Output()`. With that fix, the same Ubuntu lookup returned 407 images / 17 MiB, the runner VmHWM dropped to 103 MiB, lookup time dropped to 5.8s, and the selected image remained unchanged.

The fix merged as:

    0edccb5d3e0c3a2efa310d7a2f1725b2a201e5ee

## Remaining work

The current 2Gi Prow limit remains the mitigation until resource rollback is validated.

kubernetes/test-infra#37770 is the first 1Gi canary. It changes only the two master-only Ubuntu alpha/beta periodics and leaves the release-1.37 jobs at 2Gi.

The issue stays open until:

1. the canary package is confirmed to contain #141590;
2. both canary jobs complete five consecutive runs with clear memory headroom;
3. the standard master Ubuntu jobs are validated at 1Gi;
4. no release-1.37 job is accidentally reduced.

<details>
<summary>Original investigation</summary>

### Which jobs are failing?

These four Ubuntu DRA node jobs was OOM killed before test can start:

* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-ubuntu-dra
* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-ubuntu-dra-alpha-beta-features
* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra
* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra-alpha-beta-features

The jobs run again after kubernetes/test-infra#37491 changed the Prow memory from 1Gi to 2Gi.

This issue is for investigate the root cause. The 2Gi change only mitigate it.

### Which tests are failing?

No one test.

The Prow pod was OOM killed while `e2e_node.test remote` was preparing the run. The GCE VM was not created yet, so this was not an OOM inside Ubuntu guest.

### Since when has it been failing?

The original report in #140701 was opened on 2026-07-16.

For root cause bisect, we still need confirm the last green and first red revisions again.

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-dynamic-resource-allocation

### Reason for failure (if possible)

Known now:

* 1Gi was not enough for these Ubuntu jobs.
* 2Gi let the jobs run again.
* OOM happened in the host Prow pod before GCE VM creation.
* Ubuntu image config uses an image family and regex from `ubuntu-os-gke-cloud`.
* Before creating VM, the GCE runner calls `gcloud compute images list --format=json`.
* The command output is fully buffered, then Go unmarshals all image objects, filters it and sorts the matched images.

One possible reason is this image lookup use much more memory for the Ubuntu project than COS.

I made one local synthetic test with 250,000 image objects. The current full JSON path used about 149 MiB maximum RSS. A pre-filtered one-row input used about 1.6 MiB and selected the same image. This only show the current path can amplify memory. It does not prove the real Prow OOM root cause yet.

Proposed verification:

1. Run Ubuntu and COS with the same Kubernetes revision and 1Gi Prow limit.
2. Record cgroup `memory.current`, `memory.peak` and `memory.events`.
3. Record `/usr/bin/time -v` for `e2e_node.test` and the `gcloud` child.
4. Record the JSON output size and image count.
5. Compare current command with:

   * `--no-standard-images`
   * only `name`, `family` and `creationTimestamp`
   * a family filter when image family is configured
6. Verify both commands select the same Ubuntu and COS image.
7. Run at least three Ubuntu DRA canary jobs.

The fix is accepted when the selected image is unchanged, peak memory is reduced, and the Ubuntu jobs can complete repeatedly without OOM under the controlled limit.

### Anything else we need to know?

Related work:

* #140701 reported the original outage.
* kubernetes/test-infra#37308 reduced the node-job memory.
* kubernetes/test-infra#37309 raised it from 500Mi to 1Gi.
* kubernetes/test-infra#37491 raised it from 1Gi to 2Gi and mitigated the failure.

There is also a suspicious regex in the Ubuntu config:

```yaml
image_regex: ".*[^-cgroupsv1]$"
```

This is a negated character class. It does not mean “does not end with `-cgroupsv1`”. I think it should be checked separately because changing it together can change which image is selected and make the memory result hard to review.

I searched open and closed issues in `kubernetes/kubernetes` and `kubernetes/test-infra` with the four job names, `Ubuntu DRA OOM`, `e2e_node.test OOM` and the image project name. I did not find another issue tracking this root-cause investigation. GitHub search index can have delay.

This issue is opened separately as requested in #140701.

/sig node
/wg device-management
/kind failing-test
/assign @thc1006


</details>

One correction to my own note above, now that I've measured it. `gceImage` only keeps four string fields, so `json.Unmarshal` drops the rest of each resource, and in a local reproduction even a ~10MB test input keeps the runner process under 20MB. So the Go-side buffering is not what fills the limit.

That points at the `gcloud` child process itself, which holds and formats the whole unfiltered list before any VM exists. Family-side filtering (`--filter=family`) would cut that at the source. I'll confirm the parent/child split in the paired canary.

The canary is in and it corrects what I wrote above: I had the wrong culprit.

Numbers from pull-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd, whose image config resolves both projects:

- ubuntu-os-gke-cloud: 12558 images, 283 MiB of JSON, runner VmHWM 1067 MiB, gcloud child 380 MiB, 44.6s
- cos-cloud: 234 images, 1.5 MiB of JSON, runner VmHWM 43 MiB, gcloud child 350 MiB, 9.8s

So it is not the gcloud child, which is about the same for both. It is the runner itself. ubuntu-os-gke-cloud has 12558 images and the listing is 283 MiB of JSON; getGCEImage reads all of it through exec.Output() and json.Unmarshal expands it, and the runner peaks at 1067 MiB, past the old 1Gi. cos-cloud is 234 images and 1.5 MiB, so the same code peaks at 43 MiB. My earlier local reproduction was wrong because I modelled tiny images; the real ones are around 24 KiB each.

That also lines up with the timing: 44.6s to list and parse Ubuntu versus 9.8s for COS.

The fix is the family filter, now for a concrete reason. Passing --filter=family=<family> makes gcloud return only the family the job wants, which cuts the 283 MiB down to the handful of images that get parsed, which is what the runner buffers and unmarshals. I will send it as its own PR with a before/after on the runner VmHWM from the same job.

The #141585 canary captured the paired before/after on pull-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd, which resolves both image projects.

Before, the runner lists the whole project:

- ubuntu-os-gke-cloud: 12558 images, 283 MiB JSON, runner VmHWM 1067 MiB, gcloud child 380 MiB, 44.6s
- cos-cloud: 234 images, 1.5 MiB, runner VmHWM 43 MiB, gcloud child 350 MiB, 9.8s

After, with `--filter=family` on the same job:

- ubuntu-os-gke-cloud (pipeline-1-34-amd64): 407 images, 17 MiB, runner VmHWM 103 MiB, gcloud child 256 MiB, 5.8s
- cos-cloud (cos-117-lts): 1 image, 13 KiB, runner VmHWM 39 MiB, gcloud child 116 MiB, 2.5s

The gcloud child stays in the same range; the runner VmHWM is what moves, from buffering and unmarshaling the full Ubuntu listing. Filtering on the gcloud side brings the runner from 1067 MiB to 103 MiB and picks the same newest image, ubuntu-gke-2404-1-34-amd64-v20260824.

The fix is #141590. VmHWM is a process high-water mark, not a cgroup peak, so before the 2Gi Prow limit is lowered I would want repeated canaries and memory.peak, not this one-shot number.

RCA update. This supersedes my earlier parent/child hypotheses.

The root cause is now confirmed with paired Prow measurements from #141585.

Before the fix:

- ubuntu-os-gke-cloud:
  - 12,558 images
  - 283 MiB JSON
  - runner VmHWM: 1,067 MiB
  - gcloud child MaxRSS: 380 MiB
  - lookup: 44.6s

- cos-cloud:
  - 234 images
  - 1.5 MiB JSON
  - runner VmHWM: 43 MiB
  - gcloud child MaxRSS: 350 MiB
  - lookup: 9.8s

The Ubuntu and COS child peaks were comparable before filtering, so the child process does not explain the Ubuntu-only overflow. The difference is in the runner: getGCEImage buffers the complete gcloud stdout with exec.Output() and then unmarshals the full project listing. The 283 MiB Ubuntu response raises the runner high-water mark above the former 1Gi pod limit.

With --filter=family=<family>:

- ubuntu-os-gke-cloud / pipeline-1-34-amd64:
  - 407 images
  - 17 MiB JSON
  - runner VmHWM: 103 MiB
  - gcloud child MaxRSS: 256 MiB
  - lookup: 5.8s

- cos-cloud / cos-117-lts:
  - 1 image
  - 13 KiB
  - runner VmHWM: 39 MiB
  - gcloud child MaxRSS: 116 MiB
  - lookup: 2.5s

The selected Ubuntu image remained unchanged: ubuntu-gke-2404-1-34-amd64-v20260824.

state.title: [Failing-test]: investigate host memory used while resolving Ubuntu images for DRA node jobs
state.description:
## Current status

The root cause has been confirmed.

`getGCEImage` used:

    gcloud compute images list --format=json --project=<project>

and buffered and unmarshaled the complete project listing.

For `ubuntu-os-gke-cloud`, the real Prow measurement was:

- 12,558 images
- 283 MiB JSON
- runner VmHWM: 1,067 MiB
- lookup: 44.6s

The equivalent COS path returned 234 images / 1.5 MiB and the runner peaked at 43 MiB.

kubernetes/kubernetes#141590 added a gcloud-side family filter before the output reaches `exec.Output()`. With that fix, the same Ubuntu lookup returned 407 images / 17 MiB, the runner VmHWM dropped to 103 MiB, lookup time dropped to 5.8s, and the selected image remained unchanged.

The fix merged as:

    0edccb5d3e0c3a2efa310d7a2f1725b2a201e5ee

## Remaining work

The current 2Gi Prow limit remains the mitigation until resource rollback is validated.

kubernetes/test-infra#37770 is the first 1Gi canary. It changes only the two master-only Ubuntu alpha/beta periodics and leaves the release-1.37 jobs at 2Gi.

The issue stays open until:

1. the canary package is confirmed to contain #141590;
2. both canary jobs complete five consecutive runs with clear memory headroom;
3. the standard master Ubuntu jobs are validated at 1Gi;
4. no release-1.37 job is accidentally reduced.

<details>
<summary>Original investigation</summary>

### Which jobs are failing?

These four Ubuntu DRA node jobs was OOM killed before test can start:

* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-ubuntu-dra
* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-ubuntu-dra-alpha-beta-features
* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra
* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra-alpha-beta-features

The jobs run again after kubernetes/test-infra#37491 changed the Prow memory from 1Gi to 2Gi.

This issue is for investigate the root cause. The 2Gi change only mitigate it.

### Which tests are failing?

No one test.

The Prow pod was OOM killed while `e2e_node.test remote` was preparing the run. The GCE VM was not created yet, so this was not an OOM inside Ubuntu guest.

### Since when has it been failing?

The original report in #140701 was opened on 2026-07-16.

For root cause bisect, we still need confirm the last green and first red revisions again.

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-dynamic-resource-allocation

### Reason for failure (if possible)

Known now:

* 1Gi was not enough for these Ubuntu jobs.
* 2Gi let the jobs run again.
* OOM happened in the host Prow pod before GCE VM creation.
* Ubuntu image config uses an image family and regex from `ubuntu-os-gke-cloud`.
* Before creating VM, the GCE runner calls `gcloud compute images list --format=json`.
* The command output is fully buffered, then Go unmarshals all image objects, filters it and sorts the matched images.

One possible reason is this image lookup use much more memory for the Ubuntu project than COS.

I made one local synthetic test with 250,000 image objects. The current full JSON path used about 149 MiB maximum RSS. A pre-filtered one-row input used about 1.6 MiB and selected the same image. This only show the current path can amplify memory. It does not prove the real Prow OOM root cause yet.

Proposed verification:

1. Run Ubuntu and COS with the same Kubernetes revision and 1Gi Prow limit.
2. Record cgroup `memory.current`, `memory.peak` and `memory.events`.
3. Record `/usr/bin/time -v` for `e2e_node.test` and the `gcloud` child.
4. Record the JSON output size and image count.
5. Compare current command with:

   * `--no-standard-images`
   * only `name`, `family` and `creationTimestamp`
   * a family filter when image family is configured
6. Verify both commands select the same Ubuntu and COS image.
7. Run at least three Ubuntu DRA canary jobs.

The fix is accepted when the selected image is unchanged, peak memory is reduced, and the Ubuntu jobs can complete repeatedly without OOM under the controlled limit.

### Anything else we need to know?

Related work:

* #140701 reported the original outage.
* kubernetes/test-infra#37308 reduced the node-job memory.
* kubernetes/test-infra#37309 raised it from 500Mi to 1Gi.
* kubernetes/test-infra#37491 raised it from 1Gi to 2Gi and mitigated the failure.

There is also a suspicious regex in the Ubuntu config:

```yaml
image_regex: ".*[^-cgroupsv1]$"
```

This is a negated character class. It does not mean “does not end with `-cgroupsv1`”. I think it should be checked separately because changing it together can change which image is selected and make the memory result hard to review.

I searched open and closed issues in `kubernetes/kubernetes` and `kubernetes/test-infra` with the four job names, `Ubuntu DRA OOM`, `e2e_node.test OOM` and the image project name. I did not find another issue tracking this root-cause investigation. GitHub search index can have delay.

This issue is opened separately as requested in #140701.

/sig node
/wg device-management
/kind failing-test
/assign @thc1006


</details>

item.title: [Failing-test]: ci-kind-dra-1-34 times out before DRA suite can finish

detail.title: [Failing-test]: ci-kind-dra-1-34 times out before DRA suite can finish
detail.body:
> **Status 2026-09-14.** The comments below carry `[UPDATED]` notes and strike-through where they were wrong.
>
> - The failures are memory pressure at the 6Gi limit, not the CPU quota. Prow reports `Job pod was OOM killed by the cluster.` for both builds listed below (test container `OOMKilled`, exit 127 in the first) and for 22 of the 40 `ci-kind-dra-1-34` runs from 08-03 to 09-11, 21 of them after running into the 90 minute timeout. The kind node journals cannot see that kill, so I missed it at first.
> - The runner CPU quota problem was real but separate. kubernetes/test-infra#37733 (merged 08-21, in the job image since 09-07) copies the pod's `cpu.max` into the runner's `init` leaf. The release-1.34 binaries have `containermaxprocs=0` (`godebug default=go1.24`) and ignore it; with `GOMAXPROCS=2` in the runner env (kubernetes/test-infra#37731) my replica of the job still ran into the 6Gi limit (one run each way). Neither explains the OOM kills.
> - The apiserver leak claim is withdrawn. The memory comes from `ResourceSlice Controller creates slices`, which on release-1.34 and release-1.35 publishes 100 max-size ResourceSlices; master cut it to 10 in #136156 (1847d5b1a, "created too much load for an E2E test"). Same branch, count as the only change: about 2 GiB less non-reclaimable memory for the suite on both branches, 3.0 to 3.4 GiB in the 1.34 random seed runs that hit the scheduler log mode below.
> - Why 1.34 is worse than 1.35, and why the seed matters: the scheduler's experimental structured allocator logs the full ResourceSlice list at V(5) once per node it evaluates, per scheduling attempt (`structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go`, "Gathering pools"), about 74 MB per line while the 100 slices exist, and the jobs run kube-scheduler at `--v=5`. release-1.34 picks that allocator with the default gates (`DRAResourceClaimDeviceStatus`, beta); release-1.35 only when an alpha gate selects it (`DRADeviceBindingConditions` together with device status, or `DRAConsumableCapacity`), which the all-gates presubmit `pull-kubernetes-kind-dra-all` does. Master dropped the statement in #136588. In uncapped replays with random seeds the scheduler wrote 0.2 to 5.9 GB of log within about 30 s of that test; in job replicas at 2 CPUs, 0.2 to 4.3 GB, within about a minute at 12Gi and spread over 8 to 28 minutes in the 6Gi runs that thrashed; kube-scheduler at 1.0 to 1.7 GiB where it was sampled. With the statement deleted, the 100 slice presubmit replicas completed at 6Gi on both branches, still at 93 to 95% of the limit non-reclaimable.
> - Outcome (09-14): the remedy is the job memory, not branch code. #142082 (delete the log statement on release-1.35) and #142083 (the 100 to 10 change from #136156, release-1.35) were closed, they do not meet the cherry-pick guidelines; kubernetes/test-infra#37865 (6Gi to 12Gi for the 1.34 and 1.35 kind DRA jobs) merged on 09-14 06:25 UTC; the periodics run on a 24h interval and pick it up on their next runs, due around 14:20 UTC for `ci-kind-dra-1-34` and 20:17 UTC for `ci-kind-dra-1-35`. kubernetes/test-infra#37731 is closed. Whether the jobs stay green at 12Gi is what the next runs will show. First prow runs on the two PRs before they were closed (09-14): #142083 passed all three kind-dra presubmits; #142082 on its own passed the plain and `-all-slow` jobs; its `-all` job failed twice without an OOM kill (the first time with the apiserver stalling while the 100 slices were created and deleted, the second time on a different spec, a pod the kubelet rejected at device-plugin admission with the control plane quiet) and passed on the third run, so the log deletion alone leaves that job on the edge at 6Gi. The numbers are summarized in those PRs; I have the raw samples if anyone wants them.
>
> The original report follows, unchanged apart from the `[UPDATED]` notes, the strike-through and two heading remarks. The canary matrix and the three run rule were my own proposal at the time, superseded by the above.

### Which jobs are failing?

- https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-dynamic-resource-allocation#ci-kind-dra-1-34

I confirmed these failed runs:

- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kind-dra-1-34/2088993552422932480
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kind-dra-1-34/2082106833379528704

### Which tests are failing?

It is not only one test. The DRA suite starts but cannot finish.

One confirmed run says:

```text
Will run 66 of 7144 specs
Running in parallel across 8 processes

5 specs pass, then:

[FAILED] [847.336 seconds] [BeforeEach]
test/e2e/dra/utils/deploy.go:287

wait for service account "default" in namespace "dra-9418":
timed out waiting for the condition

Process did not finish before 1h30m0s timeout
```

There is no final `Ran N of M Specs` summary.

### Since when has it been failing?

I confirmed the two runs above.

I did not confirm the exact first bad run yet, so I do not want to give a wrong regression date. [UPDATED: the first run prow labeled as OOM-killed was on 07-14, the first run on the 07-13 kubekins image that moved dind under the pod cgroup (kubernetes/test-infra#37440).]

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-dynamic-resource-allocation#ci-kind-dra-1-34

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The primary failure is the Prow 1h30m timeout.

The job already started the tests, but namespace setup and control plane operation became very slow. One `BeforeEach` spent about 847 seconds and two namespaces could not get the default ServiceAccount in time.

The cleanup later also hit OOM or command failures around `kind export logs` and `kind delete cluster`. ~~I think this is secondary because the test process was already terminated by the Prow timeout.~~ [UPDATED: not secondary; prow reports the job pod itself as OOM-killed for this build, see the status at the top.]

Current job runs all these in one Prow container:

- Docker-in-Docker
- four kind nodes
- eight Ginkgo processes
- Kubernetes control plane
- 2 CPU
- 6Gi memory

Possible reasons (as listed at the time):

1. Eight Ginkgo processes and four kind nodes saturate the 2 CPU limit.
2. Memory reclaim makes apiserver, controller-manager or etcd very slow before OOM.
3. etcd or container storage has high I/O wait.
4. release-1.34 has a control plane or DRA regression.
5. The job downloads latest kind, and latest kind may interact badly with old release branch.
6. One DRA test or cleanup leaks cluster resources.
7. The floating latest 1.34 CI package introduced the regression.

I do not think increasing only the timeout is a good first fix.

Proposed canary matrix (superseded, see the status at the top):

| Ginkgo nodes | CPU | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 2 | 6Gi |
| 4 | 2 | 6Gi |
| 8 | 4 | 6Gi |
| 4 | 4 | 6Gi |

~~Add 8Gi memory only when `memory.events`, `memory.peak` or container metrics show memory pressure before the timeout.~~

For each run, collect:

- `cpu.stat`
- `memory.current`
- `memory.peak`
- `memory.events`
- `docker stats`
- kube-apiserver logs
- kube-controller-manager logs
- etcd logs
- time from namespace creation to default ServiceAccount creation
- final Ginkgo summary
- cleanup exit status

~~A resource or parallelism change should have at least three successful runs before merge.~~

### Anything else we need to know?

This is different from #140701.

In #140701, the Ubuntu node jobs were OOM killed before tests and before guest VM creation. In this job, the kind cluster and tests already run, then the control plane becomes too slow.

Related test-infra history:

- kubernetes/test-infra#34343 moved etcd data to `/tmp` and reduced this job memory from 9Gi to 6Gi after a canary.
- kubernetes/test-infra#37491 changed DRA node-e2e jobs from 1Gi to 2Gi. That is another job type and another failure shape.

Cleanup error handling should be a separate PR. It should preserve the primary test exit code, always try both log export and cluster deletion, and not replace the first failure with a cleanup failure.

I searched open and closed issues in `kubernetes/kubernetes` and `kubernetes/test-infra` with `ci-kind-dra-1-34`, `kind-dra-1-34`, the ServiceAccount timeout and cleanup OOM messages. I did not find an exact issue for this failure. GitHub search index can have delay.

This issue is opened separately as requested in #140701.

/sig node
/wg device-management
/kind failing-test
/assign @thc1006

comments.body:
[UPDATED 2026-09-14] Wrong conclusion. The kind node logs cannot see a pod level OOM kill. Prow's own status for this build (2088993552422932480) says `Job pod was OOM killed by the cluster.`, test container `OOMKilled`, exit 127. I struck through what no longer holds; the current picture is at the top of the issue.

I pulled the artifacts for build `2088993552422932480`, and the control plane is timing out on its own health probes ~~rather than running out of memory~~.

From `kind-control-plane/kubelet.log`, the probes fail like this:
- `kube-apiserver` readiness: TLS handshake timeout, then `context deadline exceeded`, and eventually HTTP 500.
- `etcd` and `kube-controller-manager` liveness: `context deadline exceeded`, then the controller-manager drops to `connection refused`.
- `kube-scheduler` and `coredns` go the same way.

`kube-apiserver` and `kube-controller-manager` each restart a few times (four container instances each under `artifacts/.../containers/`), and there are no `OOMKilled` events ~~anywhere~~ in the kind node logs (the pod-level kill is only visible in prow's status). ~~So this reads as CPU or I/O starvation, not memory pressure.~~ While the controller-manager is down, its ServiceAccount controller can't create the namespace's default ServiceAccount, and that's the ~847s `BeforeEach` wait in the failure.

The job packs 8 parallel Ginkgo processes and a four-node kind cluster onto a 2 CPU request/limit, ~~so the oversubscription looks like the trigger~~. ~~If that holds, the smallest experiment is one variable at a time: either raise CPU from 2 to 4, or drop Ginkgo parallelism from 8 to 4, confirmed with a few rehearsal runs before we change the job itself. A memory bump probably wouldn't help here, since nothing was OOMKilled.~~

Happy to put up a draft config change for whichever direction folks prefer.

[UPDATED 2026-09-14] The GOMAXPROCS test below is real, but it did not apply to the Prow runner of that time: the job ran in an `init` cgroup leaf with `cpu.max` = `max` (kubernetes/test-infra#37440), so a container-aware binary sized itself to the node there too. The branch explanation is struck through; the failures turned out to be memory, see the top of the issue. The three cell A/B at the end was never run.

A couple of updates after digging into why this started and why it is only 1.34.

Temporal trigger: the kubekins-e2e image this job runs was built on 2026-07-13 (`v20260713-9909545e89`, kubernetes/test-infra#37448). item.title: fix(tainteviction): retry failed pod deletions

detail.title: fix(tainteviction): retry failed pod deletions
detail.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The taint eviction controller can lose a pod eviction when the pod deletion fails after the initial deletion attempts are exhausted.

This change makes failed pod deletions durable by scheduling them on a rate-limited retry queue. Retry state is tracked per pod so stale retries do not interfere with newer eviction decisions.

The deletion path also:
- verifies the pod still exists and matches the expected UID before deletion
- avoids repeating deletion for pods that are already being deleted
- preserves the existing disruption condition handling
- uses UID preconditions when deleting a pod
- cleans up retry state when the eviction is no longer applicable

Additional unit tests cover the retry, cancellation, stale retry, pod identity, and deletion behavior.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #140639

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The change is scoped to the taint eviction controller and its timed worker support.

Validation performed locally:

- `GOCACHE=/tmp/k8s-go-build-cache go test ./pkg/controller/tainteviction -race -count=1`
- `git diff --check`

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Fixed a bug in the taint-eviction controller where pod eviction could be permanently lost after all initial pod deletion attempts failed. Failed evictions are now retried using a durable, rate-limited retry queue.
```

## Additional fixes

The `PodDeletionsLatency` metric was corrected to use
`time.Since(fireAt).Seconds()` instead of multiplying a `time.Duration`
by `time.Second`. This correction is orthogonal to the durable retry
queue implementation.

The retry path for Pods with finite `TolerationSeconds` was also corrected
so that an already-expired toleration window is not restarted during retry.
Concurrent `NotFound` responses from Pod deletion are treated as a
successful outcome rather than triggering unnecessary retry cycles.

As NamespacedName only contains namespace and name, should we include the UID?

@pacoxu 
I think we should keep the map keyed by NamespacedName.

The UID is intentionally kept in the `podEvictionItem` value and is part of the exact-item comparison in `podEvictionRetryMatches`. This gives us one current retry state per NamespacedName while ensuring a retry for an older Pod UID cannot match the current retry state after the Pod is recreated.

Including the UID in the map key would allow old and new Pod UIDs to have separate retry entries, whereas we want the newer eviction decision to replace the older retry state for the same NamespacedName.

The exact-item comparison protects stale consumers, but not stale producers; the unconditional assignment makes the last completed handoff win, which is not necessarily the newest eviction decision.

My concern is about how “newer” is determined. podEvictionRetryMatches protects the consumer side after an item has been queued, but the assignment in addPodEvictionRetry is unconditional.

@pacoxu 
Thanks for pointing this out. I’ve updated the timed worker cleanup to make worker ownership identity-aware.

Each accepted work execution now gets a unique token, and worker completion only removes the map entry when the token still matches the current entry. This prevents an older running worker from removing a newer replacement worker for the same key.

I also added a regression test covering both an immediate running worker and a scheduled worker that has already started. The test verifies that the replacement remains visible and cancellable after the stale worker completes.

The focused package tests and race tests pass locally.

state.title: fix(tainteviction): retry failed pod deletions
state.description:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The taint eviction controller can lose a pod eviction when the pod deletion fails after the initial deletion attempts are exhausted.

This change makes failed pod deletions durable by scheduling them on a rate-limited retry queue. Retry state is tracked per pod so stale retries do not interfere with newer eviction decisions.

The deletion path also:
- verifies the pod still exists and matches the expected UID before deletion
- avoids repeating deletion for pods that are already being deleted
- preserves the existing disruption condition handling
- uses UID preconditions when deleting a pod
- cleans up retry state when the eviction is no longer applicable

Additional unit tests cover the retry, cancellation, stale retry, pod identity, and deletion behavior.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #140639

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The change is scoped to the taint eviction controller and its timed worker support.

Validation performed locally:

- `GOCACHE=/tmp/k8s-go-build-cache go test ./pkg/controller/tainteviction -race -count=1`
- `git diff --check`

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Fixed a bug in the taint-eviction controller where pod eviction could be permanently lost after all initial pod deletion attempts failed. Failed evictions are now retried using a durable, rate-limited retry queue.
```

## Additional fixes

The `PodDeletionsLatency` metric was corrected to use
`time.Since(fireAt).Seconds()` instead of multiplying a `time.Duration`
by `time.Second`. This correction is orthogonal to the durable retry
queue implementation.

The retry path for Pods with finite `TolerationSeconds` was also corrected
so that an already-expired toleration window is not restarted during retry.
Concurrent `NotFound` responses from Pod deletion are treated as a
successful outcome rather than triggering unnecessary retry cycles.

comments.body:
/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm
/assign

I looked at the failure, and it appears to be a timing-boundary issue rather than a functional failure. The test expects pod deletion to complete within 5 seconds, but there have been several failures just over that threshold (e.g. ~5.1s), with the longest observed failure around 9s.

Would it make sense to relax the assertion from 5 seconds to 10 seconds? This should preserve the intended lifecycle check while allowing some scheduling/runtime variance and reducing flakiness.

@alinaqvi1129 thanks for looking. Widening the 5s bound would only address the "terminated during initialization" sub-test ([assertion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/153454f8018f6c3e1e6da09eec607f2666aa7802/test/e2e_node/container_lifecycle_test.go#L5242): 3s grace + 2s buffer). Recent misses there are all narrow:

- 5.005s: [pull-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd on PR #141971, 09-08](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/141971/pull-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd/2097678177190023168)
- 5.33s: [ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features, 09-14](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features/2099411834053332992) (passed on retry)
- 6.17s: [ci-cos-containerd-node-e2e, 09-08](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-cos-containerd-node-e2e/2097273762176045056)

However, most of this week's failures on ci-cos-containerd-node-e2e for "A pod with restartable init containers is terminating" are other sub-tests in the same Describe, with signatures that aren't timing tolerance:

- "when the PreStop hooks don't exit": `expected PreStop 2 to live for ~32 seconds, got 0` ([09-08](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-cos-containerd-node-e2e/2097198263152152576)) and `expected PreStop 1 to live for ~32 seconds, got 0` ([09-13](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-cos-containerd-node-e2e/2098944500264079360)). [Assertion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/153454f8018f6c3e1e6da09eec607f2666aa7802/test/e2e_node/container_lifecycle_test.go#L4975-L4979). The PreStop hook never recorded a start.
- "when the containers exit successfully": pod still present 70s after delete with `deletionGracePeriodSeconds: 180` ([09-09](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-cos-containerd-node-e2e/2097714672118534144)). [Assertion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/153454f8018f6c3e1e6da09eec607f2666aa7802/test/e2e_node/container_lifecycle_test.go#L4817). That's the termination hang the test exists to catch.

Source for the tallies: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#image-validation-node-e2e (162 runs, 09-07 to 09-14).

Could you take a look at those two before we change the assertion? If they turn out to be separate bugs we should split them into their own issues so this title stays accurate.

Thanks for the detailed breakdown, @harche. I'll look into the two sub-tests you flagged before changing any assertion.

For "when the PreStop hooks don't exit" — the failure message "expected PreStop 2 to live for ~32 seconds, got 0" means TimeOfStart for that PreStop hook returned zero, implying the hook never started logging at all. The assertion itself (±1500ms around 32000ms) is reasonable; the issue is that the PreStop exec process either never ran or its output wasn't captured. I'll check whether there's a race between container start/stop and the test log collector, or whether the hook exec is silently failing under crio/containerd.

For "when the containers exit successfully" — a pod still present 70s after delete with deletionGracePeriodSeconds: 180 is a genuine hang, not a timing tolerance issue. That's exactly the regression the test is there to catch. I'll look at kubelet logs from the [09-09 run](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-cos-containerd-node-e2e/2097714672118534144) to see why the pod didn't exit when its containers completed.

I'll file separate issues if these turn out to be distinct root causes. Will report back once I've dug into the logs.

detail.body:

comments.body:
/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm
/assign

My initial theory: test suite (or alternatively job's container) times out. it has 1h20m timeout and tests elapse close to it (1h16m-1h17m on avg), (job container has 1h20m timeout as well). For the latest job (5.9.26): https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-slow/2096160163231698944/prowjob.json ￼ Also total node test timeout is 1h20m, from latest job as well https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-slow/2096160163231698944: Supporting evidence: * Jobs time out after around 1h16-17m * Test seems to have been running as of August 27th, after 1.37 feature freeze was lifted, along with additional tests, and ever since the job shows failures * Before the test was added the job succeeded after on average 1h05m each time it was run (I saw mostly 59m~1h05m and even ones of 50m or 1h10m) ￼ The test was added along with at least 3 tests, so: * Given the tests run sequentially (their name contains “serial”): I asked myself how long does the test (or all 3) take (we can see in the few places it succeeded). I checked and the answers are: * `E2eNode Suite: [It] [sig-node] ImageGarbageCollect when ImageMaximumGCAge is set should not GC unused images prematurely [NodeConformance] [Serial] [Slow]` - 12m13s, 13m24s, 14m57s, 14m14s, 11m, 12m54s, 11m20s, 11m20s (again) * `E2eNode Suite: [It] [sig-node] ImageGarbageCollect when ImageMaximumGCAge is set should GC unused images [NodeConformance] [Serial] [Slow]` - 11m45s, 11m34s, 10m30s, 10m37s, 11m36s * `E2eNode Suite: [It] [sig-node] MirrorPod when recreating a static pod it should launch successfully even if it temporarily failed termination due to volume failing to unmount [NodeConformance] [Serial] [Slow]` - 6m7s, 6m2s, 6m6s, 6m3s, 6m1s (it usually passes but fails when another tests of the 3 does succeed Bottom line: the job was running fine for around 1h05m before new tests were added to it on August 27th, and after they were added it fails close to the timeout, after ~1h17m (timeout is 1h20m) wdyt?

`ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-slow` is 0 of 9 with 179 consecutive failures since 2026-09-01. ImageGC is still failing on ubuntu and cos as tracked here.

detail.title: [Flaking Test] [sig-node] ImageGCNoEviction: DiskPressure not encountered on ci-node-crio-eviction
detail.body:
### Which jobs are flaking?

`ci-node-crio-eviction` (prow job history: https://prow.k8s.io/job-history/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-crio-eviction)

Failed runs in the last two weeks (2026-08-30 to 2026-09-14, 79 runs total):

- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-crio-eviction/2098887875868233728 (2026-09-12 21:34 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-crio-eviction/2098751980372496384 (2026-09-12 12:34 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-crio-eviction/2097458984003833856 (2026-09-08 22:56 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-crio-eviction/2097255139881521152 (2026-09-08 09:26 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-crio-eviction/2097187190898429952 (2026-09-08 04:56 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-crio-eviction/2095963365972119552 (2026-09-04 19:53 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-crio-eviction/2095827467854942208 (2026-09-04 10:53 UTC)

Triage: https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?test=ImageGCNoEviction&job=ci-node-crio-eviction

### Which tests are flaking?

`E2eNode Suite.[It] [sig-node] ImageGCNoEviction [Feature:Eviction] when we run containers that should cause DiskPressure should eventually evict all of the correct pods [Disruptive] [Serial] [Slow]`

### Since when has it been flaking?

At least since 2026-09-04. 7 of the last 79 runs (~9%) failed on this test. It is the only test in the job with a repeating failure; the other eviction tests in the job each failed at most once or twice in the same window.

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-cri-o#ci-node-crio-eviction

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The test never observes the `DiskPressure` node condition and times out after 10 minutes:

```
[FAILED] Timed out after 600.000s.
Expected
    <*errors.errorString | 0xc20192b67b0>: 
    NodeCondition: DiskPressure not encountered
    {
        s: "NodeCondition: DiskPressure not encountered",
    }
to be nil
In [It] at: k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e_node/eviction_test.go:816 @ 09/12/26 22:52:42.738
```

Test timeline from the 2026-09-12 21:34 run:

```
STEP: setting up pods to be used by tests @ 09/12/26 22:42:38.701
STEP: Waiting for the expected pods to complete: [] @ 09/12/26 22:42:38.702
STEP: Waiting for node to have NodeCondition: DiskPressure @ 09/12/26 22:42:42.736
[FAILED] in [It] - k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e_node/eviction_test.go:816 @ 09/12/26 22:52:42.738
```

Environment from the failing run:

- OS image: Fedora CoreOS 44.20260817.3.2 (kernel 7.1.8-200.fc44.x86_64)
- Container runtime: cri-o://1.36.0
- Kubelet: v1.38.0-alpha.0.750+d5cbb79be9160f

The same signature appears in every one of the 7 failures. Passing runs do reach `DiskPressure`, so the pre-fill step that is supposed to push image storage over the eviction threshold is not reliably doing so on this image/runtime combination. Root cause not yet identified.

### Anything else we need to know?

- The job is currently `FLAKY` on TestGrid, not `FAILING`; the failure never hit 3 in a row.
- The closest prior issue is #130663 (ImageGCNoEviction on containerd, closed 2025-09-05). The failure mode there was different and this report is CRI-O only.
- Job config: https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/crio.yaml

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig node
